# PicoCalc Music Maker

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

A keyboard instrument for the **ClockworkPi PicoCalc**, by **Thomas Dzubin**,
written in C against the **Raspberry Pi Pico SDK** and the driver layer from
[`picocalc-text-starter`](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by **Blair Leduc** (LCD, audio and south‑bridge keyboard drivers) — vendored
here under [`picocalc-text-starter-main/`](picocalc-text-starter-main/).

```
music_maker.c               the whole program
CMakeLists.txt              builds it, reusing picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/*
                            plus picocalc-text-starter-main/songs.c (built-in songs)
pico_sdk_import.cmake        standard Pico SDK locator (copied from the starter)
picocalc-text-starter-main/  vendored driver layer + songs.c (see License; do not edit)
LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md        MIT licence; version history
CLAUDE.md                    notes for AI coding assistants
```

## What it does

1. **Splash screen** – a double‑size **PICOCALC MUSIC MAKER** title with the
   version under it, a double‑size **BY THOMAS DZUBIN** with *Built heavily on
   code by Blair Leduc (picocalc‑text‑starter)* under it (wrapped to two lines),
   then `PRESS ANY KEY TO START` and `or ESC to reboot (erases recordings)`
   under that. (The big lines are the built‑in 8×10 font scaled 2× by
   `big_text()`.)
   On this screen `ESC` reboots the PicoCalc (a plain reboot back into this
   program) **after a `REBOOT AND ERASE ALL RECORDINGS?` Y/N prompt** – the
   recordings are RAM‑only, so a reboot wipes them; `~` (SHIFT + backtick)
   reboots into **BOOTSEL** mode; a bare SHIFT/CTRL is ignored and any other
   key continues.
2. Any key opens the **Music Maker screen** (the main key loop, inline in
   `main()`); `ESC` there breaks back out to the splash. A note sounds for as
   long as its key is held. The middle of the screen is **split left / right,
   one half per speaker**, headed `LEFT CHANNEL` / `RIGHT CHANNEL` with a thin
   divider between them: each half shows the note name large (with its
   **♯ / ♭** symbol) and that channel's frequency in **Hz** centred
   underneath. A plain note looks identical on both halves; a DTMF or phone
   call-progress key shows the same symbol on each side with its low tone on
   the left and high tone on the right.

   There are **two musical-note key layouts**, toggled by the `\` key (a row‑9
   indicator shows which is live; it starts on **FULL** and stays put until a
   reboot). The **note-key rows** in the table below are the **FULL** layout;
   everything else in the table (DTMF, phone tones, arrows, transport) is the
   same in both. The **A‑G ONLY** layout makes just the `A B C D E F G` keys
   play – each sounds its own note, **SHIFT** is that note's sharp and **CTRL**
   its flat – and silences every other letter key plus `ENTER`. In the
   **A‑G ONLY** layout `H` `J` `K` also play **A B C one octave up**, so
   `C D E F G H J K` walks a full DO‑RE‑MI scale with no octave arrows (this one
   is not shown on the on‑device help screen).

   | Keys            | Sound                                             |
   |-----------------|---------------------------------------------------|
   | `\` (backslash) | switch the note-key layout: **FULL** ⇄ **A‑G ONLY** |
   | `A S D F G H J` | natural notes **A B C D E F G**                   |
   | `K` `L` `ENTER` | **A B C** one octave up – so `D F G H J K L ENTER` plays a full ascending **C‑D‑E‑F‑G‑A‑B‑C** scale with no octave arrow |
   | `Q W E R T Y U` | sharp notes **A# B# C# D# E# F# G#**              |
   | `I` `O` `P`     | **A# B# C#** one octave up                        |
   | `Z X C V B N M` | flat notes **Ab Bb Cb Db Eb Fb Gb**             |
   | `,` and `.`     | **Ab Bb** one octave up (no key for a one‑octave‑up `Cb`; `Gb` stays on `M`) |
   | **SHIFT** + `A S D F G H J K L` | the **sharp** of that key's natural note – `A#`…`G#`, and `K L` → `A# B#` one octave up |
   | **CTRL** + `A S D F G H J K L`  | the **flat** of that key's natural note – `Ab`…`Gb`, and `K L` → `Ab Bb` one octave up |
   | `0`–`9`         | the standard **DTMF** telephone digit tones       |
   | `*` and `#`     | the DTMF `*` and `#` tones                         |
   | `!` (SHIFT+1) | North American **BUSY** tone – 480 Hz left / 620 Hz right |
   | `@` (SHIFT+2) | North American **RING** tone – 440 Hz left / 480 Hz right |
   | `$` (SHIFT+4) | North American **DIAL** tone – 350 Hz left / 440 Hz right |
   | **UP arrow**    | shift every following musical note **up** one octave per press – frequency `x2` each step (`x2`, `x4`, `x8`) |
   | **DOWN arrow**  | shift every following musical note **down** one octave – a single step to `/2` only |
   | `?`             | show a full-screen **key reference** (its PLAY NOTES section matches whichever note-key layout is live); any key returns to the play screen |
   | `=`             | select the next of the 12 **song rows** (`cur_song`, wraps `0`–`11`); shown on the row‑7 status line |
   | `DEL`           | **clear** the selected song row (its notes *and* its name), after a `DELETE RECORDING n (Y/N)` confirm (`n` = the row number; only `y`/`Y` wipes it). An already-empty row is skipped silently. |
   | `ESC`           | leave the Music Maker screen and go back to the **splash screen** (breaks the inner key loop in `main()`; the outer loop redraws the splash). Recorded songs are kept. |
   | `~` (SHIFT + backtick) | reboot the PicoCalc into **BOOTSEL** (USB drive) mode. Works here and on the splash screen. Intentionally **not** shown anywhere on the device UI – the two-key combo makes it hard to trigger by accident. |

   The table above is the **Music Maker screen**. On the **splash screen** the
   same keys mean different things (see item 1): `ESC` reboots via
   `watchdog_reboot()` after the erase‑confirm, `~` still goes to BOOTSEL, a
   bare SHIFT/CTRL is ignored, and any other key opens the Music Maker screen.

   The current shift is shown near the top as `OCTAVE x2` / `OCTAVE /2` etc.
   Each press is a true octave (a factor of **2**), clamped to `/2` … `x8`;
   there is no `x3` / `/3`. Down stops at `/2` because at `/4` and `/8` every
   note is below the driver's 100 Hz floor. It does **not** affect the DTMF or
   `! @ $` phone tones (their pitches are fixed).
   Because the audio driver only makes sound between 100 Hz and 2115 Hz (its
   upper limit was raised from 2000 so the top **C7** ≈ 2093 Hz can sound), an
   extreme shift can still be displayed while being silent.

## Tuning

The 21 musical‑note pitches (7 naturals, 7 sharps, 7 flats) live in one fixed
table, `tone_freq[]` — **12‑tone equal temperament, `A4 = 440`**, taken from the
driver's `PITCH_*` macros. There is no runtime tuning switch.

```c
static const uint16_t tone_freq[NUM_TONES];   /* NUM_TONES == 21 */
```

A and B sit in octave 3, `C`–`G` in octave 4, so `A B C D E F G` is strictly
ascending; enharmonic keys (e.g. `D#` and `Eb`) share one entry. DTMF tones are
fixed and never use the table. The octave shift (UP / DOWN) then doubles or
halves the looked‑up pitch, once per key press.

## Note layers

Every key → note decision is made in one place, `map_key()`: the plain letter
rows, the dedicated sharp / flat rows (`Q…U`, `Z…M`) and the **SHIFT / CTRL**
modifier layer. The modifier layer is a small table — each row is
`{ key, its natural TONE_*, one‑octave‑up? }` — and the sharp or flat is reached
by a fixed offset into the `tone_freq[]` rows (naturals, then `+7` sharps, then
`+14` flats; a `_Static_assert` locks that order). SHIFT wins if both modifiers
are held; keys not in the table just ignore the modifiers.

Adding keys to the layer, or wiring up another modifier combination later, is a
table edit rather than new `switch` cases. The held‑modifier state is tracked in
`main()`'s key loop from the raw `KEY_MOD_SHL` / `KEY_MOD_SHR` / `KEY_MOD_CTRL`
press / release events (the south‑bridge sends letters in lower case regardless
of SHIFT / CTRL, so the layer is free to re‑interpret them).

`map_key()` also honours `note_map`, a two-value toggle flipped by the `\` key.
`MAP_FULL` is everything above. `MAP_LETTERS` handles the `a`–`g` keys directly
(keycap letter = note, `+7` / `+14` for SHIFT / CTRL), adds `h` `j` `k` → `A B C`
one octave up (an undocumented DO‑RE‑MI convenience, not on the help screen), and
returns "no note" for any other letter key, `,` `.` or `ENTER`; digits and the
`! @ $` phone tones still fall through to the shared `switch`, so telephone keys
behave the same in both layouts. `note_map` is a file‑scope `static`, so the
choice survives an `ESC`‑to‑splash round trip but resets to `MAP_FULL` on reboot.

## Recorder

A second layer on top of the instrument captures what you play. Storage is
**12 song rows** — `recbuf[REC_SONGS]` — each a 30‑character name plus a
200‑entry take, so multiple songs can be kept later.

```c
typedef struct {
    uint16_t lo;      /* left-speaker frequency  (Hz) */
    uint16_t hi;      /* right-speaker frequency (Hz) */
    uint16_t dur_ms;  /* duration in milliseconds, 1..65535  (up to ~65.5 s) */
    char     spn[4];  /* scientific pitch notation, e.g. "A#4" */
} rec_entry_t;

typedef struct {
    char        name[31];        /* song name, 30 chars + NUL ("" = unnamed) */
    int         count;           /* entries actually recorded, 0..REC_LEN    */
    rec_entry_t entry[REC_LEN];  /* the take, up to REC_LEN = 200 entries    */
} song_t;

static song_t recbuf[REC_SONGS];   /* REC_SONGS == 12 */
```

Each row carries **its own `count`**, so songs vary in length independently:
record / undo / clear and **F2 PLAY** all act on `recbuf[cur_song]` and its
`.count` (PLAY plays exactly `count` entries from that row). `=` steps
`cur_song` through `0..11` (wrapping); the selected index and that row's name
(in double quotes) show on the row‑7 status line as `SONG 3 "MY TUNE"`, and the
`n NOTES RECORDED` line switches to the new row's count. There is no
name‑editing UI yet, and save / load are still future work.

**Rows 2–11 come pre‑loaded** at startup by `load_builtin_songs()` with the ten
songs from **`picocalc-text-starter-main/songs.c`** (Blair Leduc's `songs[]`
library — *not* modified). Each `audio_note_t {left, right, duration_ms}` is
copied straight into a `rec_entry_t` (`duration_ms` via `clamp_ms`); the song's
`description` becomes the row name (`SONG 2 "Baa Baa Black Sheep"` … `SONG 11
"Twinkle Twinkle Little Star"`), and `spn` is filled by reverse‑mapping the
frequency to its note name (`freq_to_spn`, left channel, from an octave‑3‑to‑5
table). Rows **0 and 1 stay empty** for you; recording over a demo row just
replaces it (a power cycle reloads the originals).

Within a take, `lo` and `hi` are equal for a normal note; a **DTMF** or phone
call-progress key stores its two different tones (low → `lo`/left, high →
`hi`/right) so playback is the real stereo pair. A rest is `lo = hi = 0`. `spn` is the note in
scientific pitch notation using `#` / `b` — `"A#4"` = A sharp octave 4, `"C4"`,
`"Gb3"` = G flat octave 3, `""` for a rest, `"1"` / `"*"` / `"#"` for DTMF keys,
`"!"` / `"@"` / `"$"` for the phone tones — and is shown during playback (both
halves, same as live). The octave‑up keys (`K` `L` `ENTER`, `I` `O` `P`, `,`
`.`) record their bumped octave, e.g. `"A4"`, `"C5"`, `"C#5"`, `"Ab4"`.

| Key           | Action                                                          |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `F1`          | start / stop **RECORD** mode (toggle). While recording, releasing a note appends an entry `{ lo, hi, duration, spn }`. Pressing `F1` again later **without** clearing keeps appending to the same take. |
| `F2`          | **PLAY** the recording back, each entry sounding for its stored duration. The screen shows the entry the same split left / right way as live play (note + per-channel frequency on each half), with the length (`SS.HH` seconds, `.....` if somehow over 99.99 s) and an `idx / total` counter centred below. **Any key** stops playback immediately (`~` still reboots). |
| `F3` `F4` `F5` | **EDIT** / **SAVE** / **LOAD** – not implemented yet. Each just flashes a red `… FUNCTION NOT YET IMPLEMENTED` notice for ~0.5 s with a 0.5 s 1000 Hz beep. All three are greyed‑out in the on‑screen legend (`F3=EDIT F4=SAVE F5=LOAD`). |
| `DEL`         | **CLEAR** the selected song row. If the row is already empty it returns immediately; otherwise it shows `DELETE RECORDING n (Y/N)` (`n` = `cur_song`) and waits for one key — only a `y` / `Y` wipes it (`count` back to `0 NOTES RECORDED` **and** the name/description field cleared); any other key cancels. |
| `=`           | step **`cur_song`** to the next of the 12 song rows (wraps `0` → `11` → `0`). The row‑7 status line updates to `SONG n "name"`. |
| `Back`        | while recording, **erase the previous entry** (fix a wrong note). Labelled `Back` on the PicoCalc; it is the Backspace key. |
| `SPACE`       | while recording, append a **rest** – a silent gap (frequency `0`); its duration is how long `SPACE` is held. |
| `?`           | full-screen **key reference**; its **PLAY NOTES** section is drawn for the currently-selected note-key layout (FULL or A‑G). Press any key to return to the play screen. |

- Doing nothing while recording records nothing – only key presses create
  entries.
- The frequencies stored are the pitches actually produced, i.e. **after** any
  octave shift. The `spn` string keeps the **nominal** note name and octave
  (the octave shift does not rewrite it).
- A tap still stores at least `1` ms; anything past ~65.5 s is capped at
  `65535`.
- The recorder status line near the top shows `* REC  n NOTES RECORDED` while
  recording and `STOPPED  n NOTES RECORDED` otherwise, where `n` is the selected
  song's `count`. Each song holds up to `REC_LEN` = 200 entries. When a row is
  full the line turns **yellow** and reads `n NOTES (FULL)`, and every further
  note press is dropped with a short 1000 Hz chirp (`rec_push()`); the `Back`
  key frees room again.
- Two lines near the bottom of the screen name the recording-only edit keys —
  `BACK KEY = DELETE LAST NOTE` and `SPACE = RECORD A REST (SILENCE)`. They sit
  dim grey normally and turn **yellow** the moment `F1` starts recording, so a
  mis-hit is easy to take back and rests are easy to place (`show_reckeys()`).

## Known limitations

- **Nothing persists.** Recordings live only in RAM — a reboot or power‑off
  wipes them, and both `ESC` on the splash and `~` reboot. Octave shift,
  selected song and the `\` note‑map also reset on every boot.
- **`F3` / `F4` / `F5` (EDIT / SAVE / LOAD) are stubs** — they only flash a
  "not implemented" notice and beep. There is no on‑device save/load and no
  song‑name editing UI.
- **Built‑in songs share the recorder.** Rows 2–11 hold the ten `songs.c`
  tunes; recording over one replaces it until the next power cycle. Only rows
  0 and 1 are yours to start with.
- **200 entries per song** (`REC_LEN`). Past that, further notes are dropped
  (yellow `(FULL)` line + chirp); free room with the `Back` key.
- **Monophonic.** One note at a time — a second key pressed while one is held
  is ignored, and is not retriggered when the first is released.
- **Mono speaker vs. stereo tones.** DTMF and the `! @ $` phone tones put a
  different frequency on each channel; through the built‑in speaker you mostly
  hear one of the pair. Use headphones for the real sound.
- **Audible range is ~100–2115 Hz.** Notes shifted outside that window still
  show on screen but stay silent.
- **No tests / CI.** Build and flash are manual.

## Building

You need the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK toolchain (arm‑none‑eabi‑gcc, CMake, Ninja) –
exactly what `picocalc-text-starter` already builds with.

### With the Raspberry Pi Pico VS Code extension (easiest)

Open this folder (`picocalc-music-maker/`) in VS Code with the *Raspberry Pi
Pico* extension installed, then **Compile** (or *Run > Compile Project*). The
`CMakeLists.txt` here uses the same `pico-vscode.cmake` preamble as the starter,
so it picks up your installed SDK 2.2.0 / toolchain automatically.

### From a terminal

```bash
# point at your Pico SDK checkout (SDK 2.2.0; install per the Raspberry Pi
# "C/C++ SDK" docs, or let the VS Code Pico extension manage it)
export PICO_SDK_PATH=/path/to/pico-sdk

cmake -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
```

The result is **`build/picocalc-music-maker.uf2`**.

> If your PicoCalc uses a **Pico 2 / RP2350**, configure with
> `-DPICO_BOARD=pico2` (or set it in the VS Code extension). For a Pico W use
> `-DPICO_BOARD=pico_w`.

## Flashing

1. Hold **BOOTSEL** on the Pico while plugging in USB (or, if the program is
   already running, press **`~`** / SHIFT + backtick – it reboots straight
   into BOOTSEL).
2. Copy `picocalc-music-maker.uf2` onto the `RPI-RP2` / `RP2350` drive.
3. The PicoCalc restarts into the program.

## Hardware notes / pins

All pin assignments come from the reused starter drivers:

| Function            | Pins / bus                                  |
|---------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| LCD (ST7365P)       | `spi1` – SCK 10, MOSI 11, MISO 12, CS 13, DC 14, RST 15 |
| Keyboard south‑bridge | `i2c1` – SDA 6, SCL 7, address `0x1F`, FIFO reg `0x09` |
| Audio (PIO PWM)     | GP26 (left) and GP27 (right)                |

The keyboard FIFO is polled directly with `sb_read_keyboard()` so the program
sees raw **press / release** events (a note sounds while its key is held).
Because of that it does **not** call `picocalc_init()` – that would start the
starter's background keyboard poll, which drains the same FIFO.

### DTMF caveat

The starter audio driver plays one frequency per stereo channel. DTMF tones are
generated as *low tone on the left channel, high tone on the right* – summed in
headphones this is a real DTMF pair; through the mono speaker you may hear mainly
one of the two tones.

## Octaves and enharmonic notes

`picocalc-text-starter` uses scientific pitch notation, where **C** is the
lowest note of an octave. So that the `A B C D E F G` run always rises in
frequency, `A` and `B` (and their sharps/flats: `A#`, `B#`, `Ab`, `Bb`, `Cb`)
are taken from **octave 3**; `C`–`G` and their accidentals are octave 4.

`B#`, `E#`, `Cb` and `Fb` aren't on a normal keyboard row, but they were asked
for, so they play their enharmonic equivalents (`B# = C4`, `E# = F4`,
`Cb = B3`, `Fb = E4`).

### Note frequencies at every octave shift

The base column is what the key produces with no shift: `tone_freq[]` for the
`A`–`J` row, and `2 x` that for the one-octave-up keys `K` `L` `ENTER`. **UP**
then doubles once per press, **DOWN** halves once (a single step, to `/2` only) —
a true octave, never a `x3` / `/3`.

| Key → note (base SPN) | `/2` (−1) | base `x1` | `x2` (+1) | `x4` (+2) | `x8` (+3) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `A` → A (A3) | 110 | **220** | 440 | 880 | 1760 |
| `S` → B (B3) | 123 | **247** | 494 | 988 | 1976 |
| `D` → C (C4) | 131 | **262** | 524 | 1048 | 2096 |
| `F` → D (D4) | 147 | **294** | 588 | 1176 | 2352\* |
| `G` → E (E4) | 165 | **330** | 660 | 1320 | 2640\* |
| `H` → F (F4) | 174 | **349** | 698 | 1396 | 2792\* |
| `J` → G (G4) | 196 | **392** | 784 | 1568 | 3136\* |
| `K` → A (A4) | 220 | **440** | 880 | 1760 | 3520\* |
| `L` → B (B4) | 247 | **494** | 988 | 1976 | 3952\* |
| `ENTER` → C (C5) | 262 | **524** | 1048 | 2096 | 4192\* |

All values in Hz. **\*** = above the audio driver's 2115 Hz ceiling, so the note
is drawn on screen but stays silent. `/4` and `/8` are not offered: every note
there falls below the 100 Hz floor. The sharp/flat one-octave-up keys
(`I O P`, `,` `.`) work the same way — `2 x` their base tone, then the shift.
